subject: art-design
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which of the following is a complete list of the seven formal elements of art?
options: Line, shape, form, tone, texture, colour, pattern
Line, sketch, paint, print, carve, mix, shade
Balance, contrast, harmony, rhythm, unity, scale, proportion
Pencil, charcoal, ink, paint, clay, wire, paper
questions.explain: The formal elements are the visual building blocks of art: line, shape, form, tone, texture, colour and pattern.

questions.q: In the formal elements, 'tone' refers to which quality?
options: The lightness or darkness of a surface or colour
The roughness or smoothness of a surface
The temperature warmth of a colour only
The direction in which a line travels
questions.explain: Tone (or value) describes how light or dark something is, and is used to suggest three-dimensional form.

questions.q: Which set correctly lists the three primary colours?
options: Red, yellow, blue
Orange, green, violet
Red, green, blue
Black, white, grey
questions.explain: In traditional colour theory the primary colours are red, yellow and blue, which cannot be mixed from other colours.

questions.q: Two colours placed directly opposite each other on the colour wheel are described as what?
options: Complementary colours
Primary colours
Analogous colours
Monochromatic colours
questions.explain: Complementary colours sit opposite one another on the colour wheel and create strong contrast when placed together.

questions.q: Which colour is the complementary of blue?
options: Orange
Green
Purple
Red
questions.explain: Blue and orange sit opposite each other on the colour wheel, making them complementary.

questions.q: The difference between 'shape' and 'form' as formal elements is best described as which of the following?
options: Shape is two-dimensional (flat), whereas form is three-dimensional
Shape uses colour, whereas form only uses tone
Shape is organic, whereas form is always geometric
Shape is created by carving, whereas form is created by painting
questions.explain: A shape is a flat, enclosed 2D area, while form describes a 3D object that has volume and depth.

questions.q: A student wants a landscape background to feel calm and appear to recede into the distance. Which colour choice best achieves this?
options: Cool colours such as blues and greys, made paler towards the horizon
Bright warm reds and oranges applied at full intensity
Only pure black used for the whole background
Complementary colours placed side by side across the sky
questions.explain: Cool, muted colours appear to recede, so using pale blues and greys creates a calm sense of distance (aerial perspective).

questions.q: The drawing technique of building up closely spaced parallel lines to create tone is called what?
options: Hatching
Stippling
Blending
Scumbling
questions.explain: Hatching uses sets of parallel lines to build up areas of tone in a drawing.

questions.q: Which technique creates tone using a pattern of small dots?
options: Stippling
Cross-hatching
Impasto
Glazing
questions.explain: Stippling builds tone and texture from many small dots, with denser dots giving darker areas.

questions.q: In painting, 'impasto' refers to which technique?
options: Applying paint thickly so brush or knife marks stand out from the surface
Applying very thin, transparent layers of colour
Diluting paint heavily with water to make a wash
Scratching into a painted surface to reveal a layer beneath
questions.explain: Impasto is thickly applied paint that creates a raised, textured surface showing the marks of the brush or knife.

questions.q: Why would an artist use cross-hatching rather than single hatching in a drawing?
options: To build up darker, denser tones by layering lines in different directions
To make the drawing appear flatter and more two-dimensional
To add bright colour to a monochrome drawing
To smudge the lines so no marks are visible
questions.explain: Cross-hatching overlaps sets of lines at angles, increasing the density of marks to create darker tone.

questions.q: A transparent layer of paint applied over a dried colour to modify it is known as a what?
options: Glaze
Wash of gouache
Impasto stroke
Sgraffito
questions.explain: A glaze is a thin, transparent layer of paint laid over a dry underlayer to enrich or alter the colour beneath.

questions.q: A student wants to render a shiny metal jug convincingly in pencil. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Use a wide tonal range, placing strong highlights next to dark tones for sharp contrast
Use a single mid-grey tone evenly across the whole jug
Outline the jug in dark line and leave the inside blank
Use only stippling with evenly spaced dots and no tonal variation
questions.explain: Shiny surfaces show sharp contrasts between bright highlights and dark reflections, so a wide tonal range is needed.

questions.q: Lino printing (linocut) is an example of which type of printmaking?
options: Relief printing
Intaglio printing
Screen printing
Lithography
questions.explain: In lino printing the artist cuts away the areas that are not printed, so ink sits on the raised surface — a relief process.

questions.q: In a lino print, what happens to the areas that the artist cuts away from the block?
options: They stay unprinted and appear as the colour of the paper
They print as the darkest areas of the image
They collect the most ink and print solidly
They cannot be inked and so tear the paper
questions.explain: Cut-away areas sit below the surface, receive no ink from the roller, and so show as the blank paper colour.

questions.q: Carving a form out of a block of stone or wood is an example of which sculptural process?
options: Subtractive (taking material away)
Additive (building material up)
Casting from a mould
Assemblage of found objects
questions.explain: Carving removes material to reveal a form, making it a subtractive sculpture process.

questions.q: Modelling a figure by building it up from clay is best described as which type of sculpture?
options: Additive
Subtractive
Carving
Etching
questions.explain: Modelling adds and shapes material to build up a form, so it is an additive process.

questions.q: In sculpture, an 'armature' is best described as which of the following?
options: An internal framework or support inside a modelled sculpture
The polished outer surface of a finished bronze
A small preliminary sketch of the sculpture
A tool used for carving stone
questions.explain: An armature is a rigid internal skeleton, often of wire, that supports soft materials such as clay while modelling.

questions.q: Why might an artist make a monoprint rather than a lino print when they want a one-off, painterly image?
options: A monoprint typically produces a single unique print rather than an identical edition
A monoprint can only ever be printed in black ink
A monoprint requires the design to be carved into a block first
A monoprint always produces hundreds of identical copies
questions.explain: As its name suggests, a monoprint yields essentially one unique image, suiting spontaneous, painterly results.

questions.q: A student is designing a two-colour lino print. Which working method is most suitable?
options: Print the lighter colour first, then cut away more of the block and print the darker colour on top (reduction method)
Print the darkest colour first and never cut the block again
Use a single cut and print both colours in one pass without registration
Carve two separate blocks of exactly the same design and ink them identically
questions.explain: The reduction (reductive) method prints the lightest colour first, then progressively cuts the block and overprints darker colours in register.

specSource: OCR GCSE (9–1) Art & Design (J170) specification; Fine Art
